sentences.text: Glacialisaurus was a large herbivore with an estimated total length of 6.2 meters, though some estimates suggest it reached 8 meters from head to tail and weighed between 4 and 6 tonnes.
It was a robust non-eusauropod sauropodomorph, a type of dinosaur that is average in size for its group but distinct from the later, giant long-necked sauropods.
As a basal sauropodomorph, it likely possessed a long neck, a small head, and leaf-shaped teeth adapted for browsing.
Its hand was short, wide, and robust, featuring a large claw on the thumb.
The animal possessed a robust medial epicondylar crest on the femur, a trait that convergently evolved in basal theropods.

The second metatarsal features a weakly convex front border, a hypertrophied lateral plantar flange, and a robust medial distal condyle, while the first metatarsal was roughly three-quarters the length of the second.
Glacialisaurus was found approximately 650 km from the South Pole, which was located about 1000 km farther north at the time.
Fossilized tree trunks up to 2 meters high have been found in the same formation as Glacialisaurus.
Fossils of Cryolophosaurus, a pterosaur, and a tritylodont were found at the same site at an elevation of about 4100 meters.

Remains of Glacialisaurus, including a femur, incomplete ankle, and feet, were found in the Southern Hemisphere summer of 1990–1991 by Hammer and a team at Mount Kirkpatrick in the Beardmore Glacier region of the Transantarctic Mountains.
The genus is known from two specimens: a partial tarsus and metatarsus, and a partial left femur.
The fossils were sent to the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago and first reported in 1994.
The Glacialisaurus fossils remained unstudied for over ten years due to a lack of knowledge to interpret their identity.
The fossils underwent nearly three years of preparation and study by Diego Pol of CONICET and Nathan Smith of the University of Chicago.
Nathan Smith and Diego Pol described the genus and species, naming the holotype specimen FMNH PR1823.
The species was formally described and named in 2007.
Fossils of a sauropod found at the Beardmore Glacier in the same period as Glacialisaurus demonstrate that prosauropods and sauropods coexisted in the Early Jurassic.
Glacialisaurus was found alongside Cryolophosaurus, a small pterosaur, a rat-sized synapsid called Tritylodon, and an unknown theropod.
Glacialisaurus is classified as a massospondylid, a group of basal sauropodomorphs.

Glacialisaurus is frequently classified as a member of the Massospondylidae family, a group of non-eusauropod sauropodomorphs that lived from the Late Triassic to the Early Jurassic across multiple continents.
Smith and Pol identified Glacialisaurus as a massospondylid in their 2007 phylogenetic analysis.
The genus Glacialisaurus and the species Glacialisaurus hammeri were both named by Smith and Pol in 2007.
Glacialisaurus was a sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in Antarctica during the Early Jurassic period.
Glacialisaurus inhabited forests of large trees covering the then temperate Antarctica.
Glacialisaurus lived on the coast of a river flowing into the sea of the supercontinent Gondwana during the Early Jurassic.
The fossils date to the Pliensbachian stage of the Early Jurassic, approximately 186 to 182 million years ago.
Glacialisaurus lived during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 194 to 188 million years ago.
The time range for Glacialisaurus is recorded as the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian, from 199.5 to 184.2 million years ago.
Glacialisaurus lived in Antarctica during the Early Jurassic, approximately 190 million years ago.
The phylogenetic position of Glacialisaurus is considered unstable due to its fragmentary nature, though it is frequently recovered as a massospondylid.
